  --from-literal=username=admin \
  --from-literal=password='s3cr3t-p4ss'

# View a Secret (base64-encoded — not plaintext)
kubectl get secret db-credentials -o yaml

# Decode a secret value
kubectl get secret db-credentials \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d

# Mount as env var in a pod
# env:
#   - name: DB_PASSWORD
#     valueFrom:
#       secretKeyRef:
#         name: db-credentials
#         key: password

words.etymology: From Latin secretus ('set apart, hidden'); the Kubernetes Secret object is named to signal that it holds data that should be hidden from casual inspection and protected by access controls.

words.shortDefinition: A packaged collection of Kubernetes manifests with a values file, installable and upgradeable as a single unit.
words.simpleDefinition: A Helm chart is a reusable package of Kubernetes manifests. Instead of applying a dozen individual YAML files to install something like Prometheus or PostgreSQL, you install one chart with one command. Charts use a template system — you override settings in a values.yaml file, and Helm fills in the templates to produce the final YAML. Helm also tracks what you have installed (called a release), letting you upgrade, roll back, and uninstall entire application stacks as single operations.
words.longDefinition: A Helm chart is a directory (or .tgz archive) with a specific structure: Chart.yaml (chart metadata: name, version, description), values.yaml (default configurable values), and templates/ (Go template YAML files that render Kubernetes manifests using values). When you run helm install, Helm renders the templates with the merged values (defaults + any --set overrides + custom values files) and applies the resulting YAML to the cluster. The installed instance is called a Helm release — Helm stores release metadata as Secrets in the target namespace, enabling helm upgrade (re-render with new values or chart version and apply), helm rollback (revert to a previous release revision), and helm uninstall (delete all resources created by the chart). Public charts live on chart repositories (Artifact Hub is the public index). Charts support dependencies (subcharts) for bundling multiple components. The three-way strategic merge patch that helm upgrade uses computes what changed between the current release, the desired release, and any manual modifications — similar to kubectl apply's logic.
words.connector: Think of a Helm chart like an IKEA flat-pack kit — everything you need to build the finished product (application stack) is included, with an instruction booklet (values.yaml) you customize for your space (environment), and the result is assembled with one operation.
words.techContext: We use Helm charts for all third-party tools — Prometheus, Grafana, cert-manager — so a single helm upgrade updates the whole monitoring stack. Our own applications get Kustomize overlays for simpler customization.
words.exampleSentence: Installing the cert-manager chart required only two commands — adding the Jetstack chart repository and helm install — producing all 23 Kubernetes resources correctly configured with our cluster's domain.

codeExample.code:
# Add a chart repository
helm repo add prometheus-community \
  https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo update

# Install a chart (creates a Helm release)
helm install prometheus prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack \
  --namespace monitoring --create-namespace \
  --values my-values.yaml

# Upgrade a release
helm upgrade prometheus prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack \
  --namespace monitoring \
  --set grafana.adminPassword=newpass

# List releases
helm list -n monitoring

# Roll back to previous revision
helm rollback prometheus 1 -n monitoring

words.etymology: Helm is the nautical steering mechanism (tiller/wheel). The Helm project adopted the metaphor of navigating a Kubernetes cluster. A chart is a nautical navigation map — the Helm chart is your map for deploying an application.

words.shortDefinition: Linux Foundation standard defining the Image Spec, Runtime Spec, and Distribution Spec so any image runs on any runtime.
words.simpleDefinition: OCI is the set of open standards that makes container images portable. Before OCI, Docker images could only run on Docker. OCI defined a universal format for container images (how layers are structured), runtimes (how a container must be executed), and registries (how images are stored and retrieved). Any OCI-compliant image — built with Docker, Buildah, or ko — runs on any OCI-compliant runtime — containerd, CRI-O, or Podman — without modification. This interoperability is why you can build an image on your laptop and run it on any Kubernetes cluster in any cloud.
words.longDefinition: The Open Container Initiative was founded in 2015 by Docker, CoreOS, Google, Red Hat, and others under the Linux Foundation, in response to fragmentation risk as multiple container formats and runtimes competed for adoption. The OCI publishes three specifications: the Image Spec (opencontainers/image-spec) defines the container image format — a content-addressed manifest referencing an ordered list of filesystem layer blobs plus a config JSON; the Runtime Spec (opencontainers/runtime-spec) defines the interface between a container manager and a low-level runtime, specifying a config.json bundle format with namespaces, cgroups, mounts, and the process to execute; the Distribution Spec (opencontainers/distribution-spec) standardizes the HTTP registry API used to push and pull images. The reference runtime implementation is runc (donated by Docker, maintained under OCI), which accepts an OCI bundle and uses clone() + cgroups + mount + exec to create the container. Kata Containers and gVisor are OCI-compliant alternative runtimes that provide VM-level and syscall-interception isolation respectively, selectable per pod via Kubernetes RuntimeClass.
words.connector: Think of OCI like the USB standard for computers — before USB, every peripheral used a different plug. OCI standardized the 'plug' (image format and runtime API) so any container image fits any runtime without adapters.
words.techContext: Because our images are OCI-compliant, we can build them in GitHub Actions using Docker, push to ECR, and have containerd on EKS nodes pull and run them — no tool-specific knowledge required at any step.
words.exampleSentence: Switching our container runtime from Docker to containerd was completely transparent to our applications because both are OCI-compliant — the images we had already pushed to our registry ran without change.

codeExample.code:
# Inspect an OCI image manifest (using crane tool)
crane manifest ghcr.io/my-org/my-app:v1.2.3 | jq .
# {
#   "schemaVersion": 2,
#   "mediaType": "application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json",
#   "config": { "digest": "sha256:..." },
#   "layers": [
#     { "digest": "sha256:...", "size": 31234567 },
#     { "digest": "sha256:...", "size": 4567890 }
#   ]
# }

# Any OCI-compliant tool can run this image
containerd pull ghcr.io/my-org/my-app:v1.2.3
podman run ghcr.io/my-org/my-app:v1.2.3

words.etymology: Open Container Initiative is descriptively named: open (vendor-neutral, public standard) + container + initiative (an organized effort). Founded under the Linux Foundation to prevent proprietary lock-in of the container ecosystem.
